low_risk: Bladder urothelial carcinoma in this group is typically confined to the bladder wall without extensive spread. Tumors may involve the lamina propria or muscularis propria but do not extend widely into perivesical fat or adjacent pelvic organs. Differentiation is often moderate to high grade, yet the disease remains organ-confined with absent or limited lymphovascular or perineural invasion. Regional lymph nodes, when examined, are negative or only minimally involved, and extracapsular extension is not present. Surgical margins are usually free of tumor, though focal or superficial margin involvement may occasionally be seen without widespread residual disease. Distant metastasis is absent. This profile reflects disease that is clinically significant but contained within the primary site or immediate regional nodes.
intermediate_risk: Carcinomas in this category demonstrate definite invasion beyond the muscularis propria into perivesical fat, often with focal extension toward adjacent soft tissue or pelvic structures such as prostate or periprostatic tissue. They are usually high grade and frequently associated with lymphovascular invasion, with limited regional lymph node involvement possible. Margins are generally uninvolved, though tumors may approach close to the inked edges. Distant metastasis is not observed. Overall, this represents locally advanced disease with either early regional spread or high-risk histologic features, but without widespread nodal burden or systemic dissemination.
high_risk: Bladder carcinoma at this stage is aggressive and infiltrative, often large and poorly differentiated. The tumor extends beyond the bladder wall into perivesical fat and frequently into adjacent pelvic organs such as prostate, urethra, or surrounding soft tissues. Lymphovascular and perineural invasion are common, and multiple lymph nodes are typically positive for metastasis, sometimes with extracapsular extension. Surgical margins may be close or overtly involved, indicating incomplete containment. Distant metastasis may also be present or suspected. This profile represents advanced disease with high tumor burden, significant regional spread, and systemic potential, consistent with poor prognosis.

low_risk: Breast carcinoma in this group is typically confined to the breast parenchyma without frank extension into the chest wall, skeletal muscle, or skin. Tumors are usually small to moderate in size and well to moderately differentiated, with low to intermediate nuclear atypia and mitotic activity. Lymphovascular or perineural invasion is absent or minimal, and surgical margins are free of carcinoma. Regional lymph nodes are negative when examined, and cases without nodal assessment (NX) remain acceptable in this category. These findings are consistent with early-stage disease that is surgically controlled and has limited risk of systemic progression.
intermediate_risk: Tumors in this category show broader local involvement within the breast and may extend to the dermis, nipple, or superficial structures, though without extensive invasion of chest wall or systemic dissemination. Histology is often grade 2–3 with moderate to marked atypia and variable mitotic activity. Lymphovascular invasion is commonly present, and perineural invasion may also be seen. Surgical margins are close or focally involved, raising concern for residual disease. Regional lymph nodes demonstrate limited metastatic spread, typically involving up to a few nodes, sometimes with extracapsular extension. These cases represent locally advanced disease with increased risk of recurrence but remain potentially manageable with complete multimodality therapy.
high_risk: High-risk breast carcinoma is marked by aggressive morphology and extensive spread. Tumors are generally large or infiltrative, poorly differentiated (grade 3), with prominent atypia, brisk mitoses, and often necrosis. There is invasion into critical adjacent structures such as skin, nipple, or chest wall, with frequent lymphovascular and perineural permeation. Margins may be involved despite wide resection, and nodal disease is heavy, often with multiple positive or matted nodes and extracapsular extension. Distant metastasis may also be present at diagnosis. These features reflect advanced disease with high risk for systemic progression and poor prognosis without intensive treatment.

low_risk: Low-risk colorectal carcinoma typically shows well to moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma with preserved glandular architecture and only limited cytologic atypia. Tumor growth is confined to the bowel wall and pericolonic fat, with invasion not extending to adjacent organs or through the visceral peritoneal surface. Lymphovascular and perineural invasion are absent or rare. Regional lymph nodes are either entirely negative or show only minimal involvement in a single node without extracapsular spread. Surgical margins, including radial and soft tissue planes, are free of carcinoma, reflecting complete resection. Even when tumors are large or display focal mucinous change, the lack of adverse features such as multiple nodal metastases, margin involvement, or extensive invasion supports a favorable, low-risk profile.
intermediate_risk: Intermediate-risk colorectal carcinoma is characterized by moderately to poorly differentiated histology with partial loss of gland formation, variable atypia, and occasional necrosis. The tumor often extends beyond the muscularis propria into pericolonic fat, subserosa, or the visceral peritoneal surface, and may show focal invasion into adjacent structures. Vascular or perineural invasion is frequently present. Regional lymph nodes show limited metastasis, often involving one to several nodes, though sometimes absent after thorough sampling. Margins remain uninvolved in most cases, indicating technically complete excision despite locally advanced disease. Distant metastasis may be absent or limited to a single site at diagnosis. This constellation reflects an intermediate course, with controlled local disease but increased risk for recurrence or progression.
high_risk: High-risk colorectal carcinoma demonstrates aggressive morphology, including poor differentiation, mucinous or signet-ring features, and marked cytologic atypia with architectural disarray. Tumors show deep invasion through the bowel wall with direct extension into adjacent organs, perforation of the visceral peritoneum, or extensive involvement of pericolonic tissues. Lymphovascular and perineural invasion are common. Regional lymph nodes are frequently involved, often multiple, and margins may be close or positive, particularly at the radial or soft tissue planes. Distant metastases are often identified, affecting liver, omentum, or other sites. These features define biologically aggressive disease with a high likelihood of recurrence, progression, and poor clinical outcome.

low_risk: Diffuse low-grade gliomas (WHO grade II), including oligodendrogliomas and astrocytomas, typically show well-differentiated glial morphology with limited cytologic atypia and low mitotic activity. Necrosis and microvascular proliferation are absent, and proliferation indices remain low, often under 5%. These tumors infiltrate adjacent brain parenchyma in a diffuse fashion but generally lack frank invasion into deep or critical structures, and extracranial spread does not occur. Margins are difficult to define due to the infiltrative nature, though gross total resection may be achieved in some cases. When molecular testing is available, features such as 1p/19q codeletion or IDH mutation are often present and may confer more favorable prognosis.
intermediate_risk: Anaplastic gliomas (WHO grade III) display more pronounced atypia, increased cellularity, and elevated mitotic activity, with occasional microvascular proliferation but limited or absent necrosis. These tumors often extend into eloquent or midline structures such as the corpus callosum, and complete resection is rarely feasible, with residual disease common. Proliferation indices are moderate to high, usually exceeding those of grade II gliomas, reflecting greater biological aggressiveness. Margins are nearly always involved because of diffuse infiltration, though spread remains largely confined to the central nervous system without extracranial metastasis. Molecular studies may show IDH mutations or MGMT promoter methylation, but outcomes remain intermediate between low-grade gliomas and glioblastomas.
high_risk: Glioblastomas (WHO grade IV) are highly aggressive neoplasms characterized by poor differentiation, marked nuclear atypia, brisk mitotic activity, and the presence of both extensive necrosis and microvascular proliferation. They frequently infiltrate across multiple lobes or involve deep structures such as the thalamus, basal ganglia, or brainstem, often precluding meaningful resection. Surgical margins are essentially always positive due to pervasive infiltration, and residual disease is expected. Proliferation indices are high, and molecular features such as IDH-wildtype status and EGFR amplification are common, correlating with poor prognosis. Though extracranial metastasis is rare, leptomeningeal dissemination may occur, underscoring the aggressive clinical behavior.

low_risk: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma in this category is generally small to moderate in size and shows well to moderately differentiated histology with preserved squamous features and limited atypia. Invasion is confined to the mucosa or superficial soft tissues, or may show only focal extension into adjacent structures without frank involvement of bone, cartilage, or deep musculature. Lymphovascular and perineural invasion are absent or limited. Surgical margins are free of tumor or narrowly clear. Regional lymph nodes are negative for metastasis when examined, or not sampled, and there is no evidence of distant spread. The overall profile corresponds to early-stage disease with favorable prognosis.
intermediate_risk: Tumors in this group are typically moderate to large and often show moderately to poorly differentiated histology, with greater nuclear atypia and variable keratinization. They demonstrate invasion into deeper soft tissues, minor salivary glands, or bone/cartilage, but without diffuse or destructive extension into multiple compartments. Lymphovascular and/or perineural invasion is more frequently encountered. Surgical margins are usually negative but may be close, and regional lymph nodes often contain a limited number of metastases, sometimes with early extranodal extension. Distant metastasis is not identified. The disease generally corresponds to locally advanced stage with moderate nodal burden and intermediate prognosis.
high_risk: High-risk head and neck squamous cell carcinoma is characterized by large size, poorly differentiated morphology, and aggressive histologic features such as marked atypia, necrosis, and brisk mitotic activity. There is extensive invasion into bone, cartilage, salivary tissue, or deep soft tissue planes. Lymphovascular and perineural invasion are common, and surgical margins may be close or overtly involved. Nodal disease is substantial, with multiple lymph nodes positive and frequent extranodal extension. Distant metastasis may be present or suspected. The pathologic stage corresponds to advanced disease with high risk of recurrence and poor prognosis.

low_risk: Renal cell carcinoma in this group remains largely confined to the kidney, with growth limited to the renal parenchyma or focal extension into renal sinus or perinephric tissues but without frank invasion of adjacent organs. Tumors are typically small to moderate in size and demonstrate low to intermediate nuclear grade, though higher grade areas may be present without translating into aggressive spread. Lymphovascular and perineural invasion are absent or minimal. Surgical margins are uninvolved, and regional nodes are negative when examined or not assessed (Nx). Distant metastasis is not documented. This constellation reflects localized disease with indolent or controlled features despite occasional high-grade morphology.
intermediate_risk: Renal cell carcinoma at this level shows evidence of more advanced local disease, including extension into the renal capsule, sinus, perinephric fat, or renal vein, but without unequivocal invasion into adjacent organs. Tumors are often moderate to large in size, with intermediate to high nuclear grade and variable necrosis. Lymphovascular invasion is more common, and resection margins are negative though sometimes close. Regional nodes may be limitedly positive when sampled, or not assessed. Distant metastasis is absent or not clearly reported. These cases correspond to locally advanced but surgically resectable carcinoma with features that confer increased risk of progression.
high_risk: Renal cell carcinoma in this group demonstrates aggressive biological and morphological behavior. Tumors are usually large and high grade, with marked atypia, necrosis, and invasion extending beyond the kidney into perinephric tissues, renal sinus, major vessels, or directly into adjacent organs. Lymphovascular invasion is frequent, margins may be close or focally involved, and regional lymph nodes are often positive, sometimes with extracapsular extension. Distant metastases are common, involving organs such as lung, bone, adrenal, or liver. This profile reflects advanced or disseminated disease with poor prognosis and high risk of recurrence or progression.

low_risk: Papillary renal cell carcinoma in this category is confined to the kidney without extension beyond the renal parenchyma or capsule. Tumors are usually well to moderately differentiated, with limited nuclear atypia, absent or minimal necrosis, and low mitotic activity. Invasion of perinephric or sinus fat, adrenal gland, or major vessels is not identified. Lymphovascular and perineural invasion are absent, and surgical margins, including vascular and soft tissue margins, are uninvolved. Regional lymph nodes, when sampled, are negative for metastasis; cases with NX status are acceptable if no evidence of spread is present. Distant metastasis is not described. These features represent localized, organ-confined disease with a favorable profile.
intermediate_risk: Tumors in this group demonstrate locally advanced features while remaining limited to Gerota’s fascia. Carcinoma may invade into perinephric or renal sinus adipose tissue and can extend into the renal vein or pelvis, though without spread beyond Gerota’s fascia or into adjacent organs. Differentiation is moderate to high grade with variable atypia, and focal necrosis is often seen. Lymphovascular invasion is commonly present, and regional lymph nodes may be involved by metastasis, sometimes with perinodal extension, although the number of positive nodes is limited. Surgical margins are generally negative but may be close or occasionally positive at vascular sites. Distant metastasis is not identified. Overall, these findings indicate disease that has progressed beyond the kidney but remains regionally confined.
high_risk: High-risk papillary renal cell carcinoma is characterized by poorly differentiated or sarcomatoid morphology, marked nuclear atypia, and frequent necrosis. The tumor shows aggressive local invasion, extending beyond Gerota’s fascia into adjacent organs, adrenal gland, or major vascular structures such as the renal vein and inferior vena cava. Lymphovascular involvement is extensive, and surgical margins, particularly vascular margins, may be positive. Multiple regional lymph nodes are usually involved, often with extracapsular extension, and nodal burden is typically high. Distant metastases may also be present. Together, these features define advanced, aggressive disease with systemic risk.

low_risk: Hepatocellular carcinoma in this category is typically solitary and confined within the liver parenchyma, without invasion into major vascular structures, bile ducts, or adjacent organs. Tumors are usually well to moderately differentiated, with limited cytologic atypia and absent or minimal necrosis. Lymphovascular and perineural invasion are not identified, and surgical resection margins are uninvolved by tumor with adequate clearance. Regional lymph nodes, when sampled, are negative for metastasis, though many cases are NX. Distant spread is not described. Overall, these tumors correspond to localized disease with complete resection and favorable histopathologic features.
intermediate_risk: Hepatocellular carcinoma in this group may be multifocal or moderately advanced in size, and the histology often shows moderate to poor differentiation. Microvascular invasion or capsular infiltration is commonly present, and small-vessel or early portal venous involvement may be identified, but there is no gross vascular thrombus or frank extension into adjacent organs. Necrosis or satellite nodules can occur, but the tumor remains largely contained within the liver. Surgical margins are generally free of carcinoma, though some margins may be close or indeterminate. Regional lymph nodes are usually negative or not sampled, with only rare limited involvement possible. Distant metastasis is not evident, but the disease reflects a higher-risk localized or regionally advanced stage with more aggressive histology and vascular involvement.
high_risk: Hepatocellular carcinoma in this category demonstrates large or multifocal disease, often with a dominant mass and additional satellite nodules. Tumors are usually poorly differentiated or show aggressive histologic patterns, with high proliferative activity and necrosis. Extensive vascular invasion, including major vessel involvement or tumor thrombus, is frequent, and direct extension into the capsule or adjacent structures may occur. Surgical margins may be close or involved, and regional lymph nodes can show metastasis, with or without extracapsular extension. While distant metastasis is variably reported, spread to lung, bone, or peritoneum is possible. These features indicate advanced pathological stage, aggressive biology, and a high risk of recurrence or progression.

low_risk: Early-stage lung adenocarcinoma in this category typically presents as a small to moderate lesion that is well to moderately differentiated, though focal areas of higher-grade morphology may be seen. Invasion is usually limited to the visceral pleura or confined to adjacent parenchyma without frank extension into mediastinal or chest wall structures. Lymphovascular or perineural invasion is absent or minimal, and resection margins are free of carcinoma. Regional lymph nodes, when sampled, are generally negative or only rarely show limited involvement without extracapsular extension; cases with NX status may also be included if no adverse features are described. Distant metastasis is not identified, and the overall profile is consistent with localized, resected carcinoma carrying a relatively favorable prognosis.
intermediate_risk: Intermediate-risk tumors show more advanced features, with moderate to poor differentiation and a greater likelihood of pleural or bronchial involvement. Invasion often extends into the visceral pleura or bronchial wall and may approach but not extensively breach adjacent mediastinal structures. Lymphovascular invasion is frequently identified, and regional lymph node metastasis is present in some cases, though nodal burden remains limited and extracapsular spread is generally absent. Margins are usually negative, but close margins may be noted. No evidence of distant metastasis is typically seen. This pattern reflects regionally advanced disease where resection has controlled gross spread but important adverse risk factors remain.
high_risk: High-risk lung adenocarcinomas are characterized by large or infiltrative tumors with poor differentiation, extensive atypia, and high proliferative potential. These tumors frequently extend beyond the pleura into adjacent organs or mediastinal structures, or they involve major bronchi with destructive growth. Lymphovascular and perineural invasion are common, and nodal metastasis is frequent, often with multiple nodes involved or extracapsular extension. Surgical margins may be close or overtly involved, and distant metastasis may also be present. Collectively, these features define aggressive, advanced-stage disease associated with a high likelihood of recurrence and poor clinical outcome.

low_risk: Lung squamous cell carcinoma in this group remains confined to the lung parenchyma or bronchial tree without frank invasion into the chest wall, mediastinum, or diaphragm. Tumors are generally small to moderate in size and show well to moderately differentiated histology, sometimes with focal poor differentiation but without extensive atypia or necrosis. Lymphovascular or perineural invasion is absent or minimal, and resection margins are clear. Regional lymph nodes, when examined, are negative for metastasis, and NX status is acceptable. Distant spread is not identified. These findings correspond to early-stage, completely resected disease with a favorable prognosis.
intermediate_risk: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung in this category demonstrates moderately to poorly differentiated morphology, often with invasion into visceral pleura, bronchus, or peribronchial tissue, and occasionally into chest wall or rib but without diffuse mediastinal or diaphragmatic involvement. Lymphovascular or perineural invasion may be present, and a limited number of regional lymph nodes can be positive for metastasis, though margins are usually negative. Distant metastasis is not seen. These tumors represent locally advanced disease with restricted nodal or structural spread but retained surgical control.
high_risk: High-risk lung squamous cell carcinoma is characterized by poorly differentiated histology, often with large or infiltrative growth, extensive atypia, necrosis, and frequent mitoses. The tumor extends beyond the lung parenchyma into pleura, chest wall, or mediastinum, and margins may be close or involved. Regional lymph nodes are frequently positive for metastasis, sometimes with extracapsular extension, and lymphovascular invasion is common. Distant metastasis may be present or cannot be excluded. This pattern reflects aggressive, advanced disease with poor prognosis.

low_risk: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas in the low-risk category are typically well to moderately differentiated, retaining glandular morphology with limited cytologic atypia. Tumors are often confined to the pancreas or show focal extension into adjacent soft tissue, duodenal wall, or periampullary structures, but without gross invasion of major vessels. Lymphovascular and perineural invasion may be absent or only focal. Regional lymph nodes are negative when examined, or only rarely show isolated involvement without extracapsular spread. Resection margins are uninvolved or narrowly clear, and distant metastasis is not present. The overall profile reflects a lesion that, while invasive, remains locally controlled and surgically manageable.
intermediate_risk: Intermediate-risk pancreatic adenocarcinomas usually demonstrate moderately to poorly differentiated histology with irregular glandular architecture and more pronounced nuclear atypia. They frequently extend beyond the pancreas into peripancreatic fat, duodenal wall, or periampullary tissues, though without frank encasement of major vascular structures. Lymphovascular and/or perineural invasion is often present, and a limited number of regional lymph nodes may be positive for metastasis, but extracapsular extension is uncommon. Surgical margins are generally free or close, with retroperitoneal or vascular-adjacent margins sometimes at risk. No distant metastases are identified. This pattern reflects locally advanced disease with regional spread, but without the fully aggressive features of high-risk tumors.
high_risk: High-risk pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas are characterized by poor differentiation, often with solid or infiltrative growth, marked atypia, necrosis, and brisk mitotic activity. They invade extensively into surrounding structures, including peripancreatic soft tissue, duodenum, bile duct, or major vascular grooves, and frequently involve multiple anatomic planes. Lymphovascular and perineural invasion are almost always present. Margins are often involved, especially at the retroperitoneal or uncinate/vascular margins, despite attempted complete resection. Regional lymph node metastasis is common, often with multiple nodes involved, and extracapsular extension may be present. Distant metastasis may also occur, signifying aggressive biology and advanced stage. This constellation of features places the disease in the highest risk tier with poor prognosis.

low_risk: Cutaneous melanoma in this category is typically thin and localized, with limited growth and relatively indolent features. The lesion is confined to the epidermis and superficial dermis without invasion into deeper soft tissue or adjacent structures. Ulceration is absent, mitotic activity is low, and necrosis is not observed. Lymphovascular or perineural invasion is not identified. Regional lymph nodes, when examined, are negative, and NX status is acceptable. Surgical margins are uninvolved, reflecting complete excision. No distant metastasis is reported. Overall, this represents an early-stage melanoma with favorable histologic and clinical features.
intermediate_risk: Melanomas in this group are of moderate thickness and show more pronounced atypia, sometimes with ulceration or increased mitotic activity. The tumor may extend into the deep dermis or superficial subcutaneous tissue but does not demonstrate extensive invasion of critical adjacent structures. Lymphovascular or perineural invasion may be present but limited. Surgical margins are usually negative after wide excision. Regional lymph nodes may be involved to a limited extent, such as a small number of positive sentinel or regional nodes, though extracapsular extension is not prominent. Distant metastasis is not identified. These cases generally correspond to intermediate pathologic stages, reflecting localized or regionally advanced disease with controlled surgical management.
high_risk: High-risk melanomas are characterized by thick, aggressive growth with poor differentiation, extensive atypia, and frequent ulceration. The tumors invade deeply into subcutaneous tissue, skeletal muscle, or adjacent anatomic structures, and lymphovascular or perineural invasion is common. Regional nodal metastases are multiple or bulky, often with extracapsular extension. Surgical margins may be close or involved, raising concern for residual disease. Distant spread is frequent, including visceral or brain metastases. Proliferative indices such as Ki-67 are often markedly elevated, and necrosis is commonly observed. Clinically, this represents advanced, biologically aggressive melanoma with high risk of recurrence and poor prognosis.

low_risk: Low-risk gastric adenocarcinoma is generally characterized by disease that, while it may be moderately to poorly differentiated, remains localized in extent. Tumor invasion is confined to the mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, or subserosal adipose tissue without definite penetration into adjacent organs. Regional lymph nodes are negative for metastasis when sampled, or lymph node status is not reported, allowing NX to remain compatible with this category. Surgical margins are uninvolved, and distant metastasis is absent. Vascular or perineural invasion may be absent or only focal, but overall the disease is resectable and remains controlled within the primary gastric wall and immediate perigastric tissues.
intermediate_risk: Intermediate-risk gastric adenocarcinoma demonstrates moderately to poorly differentiated morphology with more extensive penetration through the gastric wall into perigastric fat, serosa, or occasionally contiguous structures without diffuse adjacent organ invasion. Regional lymph node metastasis is present, often involving a limited to moderate number of nodes, with extracapsular extension reported in some but not all cases. Lymphovascular and perineural invasion are frequently identified. Surgical margins are typically negative, and no distant metastasis is documented. This pattern reflects locally advanced disease with moderate nodal burden and higher risk of recurrence, though complete surgical resection is usually achieved.
high_risk: High-risk gastric adenocarcinoma is defined by aggressive morphology, often poorly differentiated with marked cytologic atypia and high proliferative activity. Tumors extend through the gastric wall with frank invasion into adjacent organs, peritoneal surfaces, or omental tissue, or they present with extensive nodal involvement including multiple positive regional nodes, frequently with extracapsular extension. Surgical margins may be close or positive, and distant metastasis may be present. Vascular and perineural invasion are common. These findings collectively indicate advanced, aggressive disease with high potential for recurrence and systemic spread despite surgical intervention.

low_risk: Endometrial carcinomas in this category are typically confined to the endometrium or show only superficial myometrial invasion without extension into cervical stroma, adnexa, or parametrial tissues. Tumors are usually small and well to moderately differentiated (FIGO grade 1–2) with limited atypia, although focal high-grade features may occasionally be present without extensive spread. Lymphovascular and perineural invasion are absent or not identified, and surgical margins are negative or widely clear. Regional lymph nodes, when examined, are negative for metastasis, and NX status is acceptable if no nodes are submitted. No extracapsular extension or distant metastasis is described. Proliferative activity is low to moderate, necrosis is absent or focal, and immunoprofiles often show hormone receptor positivity. These findings reflect localized disease with limited biologic aggressiveness.
intermediate_risk: Intermediate-risk tumors are generally moderately to poorly differentiated (FIGO grade 2–3) and of moderate to large size. They commonly show invasion into the myometrium beyond the inner half or involve the cervical stroma, with occasional spread to adnexa, serosa, or omentum, but without unequivocal parametrial or bladder/rectal wall invasion. Lymphovascular space invasion is frequently present, though perineural invasion is uncommon. Surgical margins are negative or only close. Regional lymph nodes are usually examined and are either negative or show only limited involvement without extracapsular extension, though NX status may also occur. Distant metastasis is absent or limited to peritoneal implants. Proliferative indices and necrosis are variable, but higher than in low-risk tumors. Immunohistochemistry may reveal variable ER/PR expression, focal p53 or MMR abnormalities, or molecular alterations such as PTEN or PIK3CA mutations. This profile represents disease that is locally advanced or shows limited nodal spread, but remains potentially controllable.
high_risk: High-risk endometrial carcinomas include poorly differentiated endometrioid tumors (FIGO grade 3) as well as serous and clear cell histologies. These tumors are usually large, deeply invasive into the myometrium, and extend into cervical stroma, adnexa, parametria, or serosal surfaces, with occasional invasion into bladder or rectum. Lymphovascular invasion is common and often extensive, and perineural invasion may be present. Surgical margins may be close or overtly involved. Regional lymph node metastases are frequent and often multiple, sometimes with extracapsular extension. Distant metastases, including peritoneal, omental, or pulmonary deposits, may be present. Necrosis is common, mitotic activity is high, and treatment effect is generally poor or absent. Immunoprofiles often show aberrant p53 expression, MMR deficiency, or strong p16 positivity, and molecular testing may reveal high-risk alterations such as TP53 mutations or HER2 amplification in serous types. These features reflect aggressive biology with a high likelihood of recurrence and systemic spread.
